content:
Some legacies are carved in stone. Others are built into the daily rhythm of a campus — a bench where students rest between classes, a tree that will shade them for decades. Laredo College chose both when it honored the late Carolyn M. Schmies with a memorial bench and magnolia tree dedication, according to the college's official announcement.

The ceremony placed Schmies' bench alongside the bench honoring her beloved daughter, Cesha Monique Brown — a quiet, permanent reminder that the two will keep watching over new generations of Palominos.

The tributes did not stop at symbolism. Her husband, Kenneth R. Schmies — a member of the Laredo College Education Foundation — announced a $500 annual scholarship to support a student with special needs, carrying forward her lifelong devotion to education.

Laredo College President Dr. Minita Ramírez praised Schmies as a cherished member of the Palomino family whose kindness and compassion touched everyone around her, saying the bench honors not only her years of service but a life dedicated to lifting people up.

The magnolia tree beside the bench was donated by Leadership Women, an organization devoted to cultivating women leaders. Its chief operating officer, Heidi K. Murray, said Schmies' involvement in the group's state, national and international efforts left a lasting mark, and that the tree would carry her memory forward.

Schmies' trail was blazed long before she arrived in Laredo. After beginning her career as an Indianapolis sixth-grade teacher, she moved to General Motors, where — despite her young age — she became the company's first female and African-American supervisor, and later its first female buyer. She went on to lead at GM/Delphi across the U.S. and Mexico.

She began at Laredo College's South Campus as an adjunct speech instructor and rose fast: within months she held a full-time post, within a year she chaired the Reading and Communication Department, and in 2019 she became Interim South Campus Dean — then Dean of the South Campus. She retired in 2021 after 12 years of service but kept giving through charitable work.

Her civic footprint in Laredo was just as deep: president of the United Way of Laredo, president of Literacy Volunteers of Laredo, vice president of the Optimist Club, Leadership Women regional ambassador for Laredo, board member of the Holding Institute and chair of the Laredo College United Way Committee.

For a woman who spent her career opening doors — at a car plant, in a classroom, across a border community — a bench and a tree feel exactly right.

Sources: Laredo College official announcement (laredo.edu), Oct. 18, 2026.

title: A bench, a tree, and a scholarship: Laredo College honors trailblazer Carolyn Schmies
